Superior means toward the head, or above, and inferior means toward the feet, or below. The nose is superior to the mouth.

Anterior means toward the front of the body and posterior toward the back. They are also called ventral and dorsal. The breastbone (sternum) is anterior to the heart, and the spinal column (the backbone) is posterior to it.

Medial means toward the midline, the imaginary line down the middle of the body, and lateral means away from it. The nose is medial to the eyes, and the ears are lateral to them.

Proximal means nearer the trunk (the main part of the body: the chest, belly and back), or nearer the point where a limb attaches, and distal means farther from it. They describe places along an arm or a leg. To compare two parts of the head, such as the eyes and the mouth, use the other pairs, such as superior and inferior. The elbow is proximal to the wrist, and the fingers are distal to it.

Superficial means near the body surface and deep means farther inside. The skin is superficial to the muscles.

teachingSections.heading: Three planes
teachingSections.body:
A plane is an imaginary flat surface that cuts the body into two parts. Anatomy uses three main planes.

A sagittal plane divides the body into left and right parts. One that runs exactly down the middle, making equal left and right halves, is called the midsagittal plane.

A frontal plane, also called a coronal plane, divides the body into front and back parts.

A transverse plane, also called a horizontal plane, divides the body into upper and lower parts.

teachingSections.heading: The body cavities
teachingSections.body:
A body cavity is a space inside the body that holds organs.

The cranial cavity, inside the skull, holds the brain. The spinal cavity, inside the backbone (the column of bones called vertebrae), holds the spinal cord.

The thoracic cavity is the chest. It holds the heart and lungs, and the rib cage surrounds it. Its floor is the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle that separates the thoracic cavity above from the abdominal cavity below.

The abdominal cavity holds the stomach, the liver and most of the intestines. Below it is the pelvic cavity, inside the pelvis (the ring of bones formed by the hip bones and the base of the spine), which holds organs including the urinary bladder. Together the abdominal and pelvic cavities are called the abdominopelvic cavity.

additionalExamples.setup: Where is the urinary bladder?
additionalExamples.strong: In the pelvic cavity, the lowest part of the abdominopelvic cavity, below the abdominal cavity.
additionalExamples.explanation: The bladder sits low in the trunk, inside the pelvis, so it is in the pelvic cavity, the lowest part of the abdominopelvic cavity, below the abdominal cavity.

additionalExamples.setup: A cut down the middle of the body, from between the eyes to between the feet. Which plane?
additionalExamples.strong: A sagittal plane, which divides the body into left and right. Because it runs exactly down the middle, it is the midsagittal plane.
additionalExamples.explanation: Say which two parts the cut separates, then name the plane: left and right is sagittal, front and back is frontal (coronal), upper and lower is transverse.

misconception.wrongModel: Left and right mean the left and right side of the picture.
misconception.whyItFails: Anatomy diagrams usually show a person facing you, so the person’s left side is on your right. Reading left and right from the page puts structures on the wrong side of the body.
misconception.betterModel: Always use the person’s own left and right. Picture yourself in the diagram, facing out, and name the sides from there.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading proximal and distal as “close to” and “far from” each other.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Both terms measure distance from where the limb joins the trunk, not from each other. “The wrist is proximal to the fingers” says the wrist is nearer the trunk than the fingers are. It says nothing about how close the wrist is to the fingers.
commonMistakes.fix: On an arm or a leg, ask which of the two structures is nearer where the limb joins the trunk. That one is proximal.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing up the frontal and sagittal planes.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: They run at right angles to each other. A frontal plane runs from side to side and separates front from back. A sagittal plane runs from front to back and separates left from right.
commonMistakes.fix: Say which two parts the plane separates before you name it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting the stomach in the chest cavity.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The diaphragm is the boundary. The heart and lungs are above it, in the thoracic cavity. The stomach and liver are below it, in the abdominal cavity, even though they sit high in the abdomen.
commonMistakes.fix: Find the diaphragm first, then ask whether the organ is above it or below it.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Name the main bones by region, tell tendons from ligaments, divide the nervous system, and place the skin among the organs.

lesson.title: Bones, Muscles, Nerves and Skin
lesson.summary: Name the main bones by region, tell tendons, ligaments and cartilage apart, divide the nervous system and the brain, and learn why the skin counts as an organ.

content.objective: Name the main bones by body region, say what tendons and ligaments connect, divide the nervous system into its central and peripheral parts, place the parts of the brain, and describe the skin as an organ.
content.explanation:
Bend your arm and feel your upper arm. Under the skin is muscle, and under the muscle is bone. Most muscles are attached to bones by tendons, tough cords of tissue. Where two bones meet at a joint, bands called ligaments hold them together. The names matter because questions often ask exactly what joins what.

This lesson covers four systems: the skeleton that gives the body its frame, the muscles that move it, the nervous system that controls it, and the skin that covers it. The skeletal system is the bones, plus the cartilage and ligaments at the joints. The muscular system is the muscles, most of them attached to the bones by tendons. The nervous system is the brain, the spinal cord and the nerves. The integumentary system is the skin, together with the hair and nails.

The direction words from the body map lesson come back here. You will use them to say where the cerebellum sits compared with the rest of the brain.
content.whyMatters: Questions on these systems often offer a very similar wrong answer: a ligament for a tendon, the wrist bones for the ankle bones, the peripheral nervous system for the central one. Knowing what each structure connects to, and where it sits, is what tells the right answer from the near miss.
steps: Decide which system the question is about: bones, muscles, nerves or skin.
For a bone, name the body region first, then the bone in that region.
For a connecting tissue, ask what it joins: muscle to bone is a tendon, bone to bone is a ligament.
For the nervous system, ask whether the structure is the brain or spinal cord (central) or a nerve outside them (peripheral).
For a position question, use the direction pairs from the body map lesson.

workedExample.prompt: A diagram of the knee labels a tough band that joins the thigh bone to the shinbone. Is it a tendon or a ligament? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: A tendon. Tendons are the tough cords you find around the knee.
workedExample.strongAnswer: A ligament. Check what it joins: the thigh bone (femur) and the shinbone (tibia) are both bones, and tissue that joins a bone to a bone is a ligament. A tendon joins a muscle to a bone.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer goes by where the tissue is, but tendons and ligaments are both found around the knee. The strong answer asks what the band connects, which is the only thing that decides its name.

guidedQuestion.prompt: A tough cord attaches the biceps muscle to a bone of the forearm. What is it called?
choices: A ligament
Cartilage
A tendon
A nerve
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: A tendon
guidedQuestion.hint: What does it join: muscle to bone, or bone to bone?
guidedQuestion.explanation: A tendon joins a muscle to a bone, and this cord joins the biceps muscle to a bone, so it is a tendon. A ligament joins a bone to a bone. Cartilage is the smooth tissue covering the ends of bones in many joints, and a nerve carries signals rather than joining one structure to another.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which group of bones sits in the ankle?
choices: The carpals
The tarsals
The phalanges
The vertebrae
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The tarsals
practiceQuestions.hint: Carpals and tarsals are a matching pair, one near the hand and one near the foot.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The tarsals are the bones of the ankle. The carpals are the matching bones of the wrist. The phalanges are the bones of the fingers and toes, and the vertebrae form the spinal column.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What do the skull and the rib cage have in common?
choices: Both are made of cartilage
Both are part of the spinal column
Both are found in the limbs
Both enclose and protect organs
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Both enclose and protect organs
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about what sits inside each one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The skull encloses and protects the brain, and the rib cage encloses and protects the heart and lungs. Both are made mainly of bone, not cartilage. The spinal column is made of the vertebrae, and neither the skull nor the ribs is in the arms or legs.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these is part of the peripheral nervous system?
choices: A nerve in the arm
The brain
The spinal cord
The cerebellum
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A nerve in the arm
practiceQuestions.hint: The central nervous system is the brain and the spinal cord. What is left?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A nerve in the arm is outside the brain and spinal cord, so it is part of the peripheral nervous system, which is all the nerves outside those two. The brain and the spinal cord make up the central nervous system, and the cerebellum is part of the brain.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which part of the brain is the largest?
choices: The cerebellum
The brainstem
The cerebrum
The spinal cord
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The cerebrum
practiceQuestions.hint: The cerebellum is a smaller part that sits below and behind the largest one. Which part is that?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. The cerebellum is a smaller part below and behind it, and the brainstem connects the rest of the brain to the spinal cord. The spinal cord is not part of the brain at all, though it is part of the central nervous system.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The skin counts as an organ. Which body system is it part of?
choices: The skeletal system
The nervous system
The digestive system
The integumentary system
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The integumentary system
practiceQuestions.hint: This system also includes the hair and nails.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The skin belongs to the integumentary system, together with the hair and nails. The skeletal system is the bones and the cartilage and ligaments at the joints, the nervous system is the brain, spinal cord and nerves, and the digestive system is the tract that food passes through, with the organs beside it.

masteryCheck.prompt: Where is the cerebellum compared with the cerebrum?
choices: Superior and anterior to it
Inferior and posterior to it
Superior and posterior to it
Inferior and anterior to it
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Inferior and posterior to it
masteryCheck.hint: Two direction words give two facts: is it above or below the cerebrum, and in front of it or behind it?
masteryCheck.explanation: The cerebellum lies below and behind the cerebrum. Below is inferior and behind is posterior, so it is inferior and posterior to the cerebrum. Superior would put it above the cerebrum, and anterior would put it in front, so each other choice gets at least one of the two directions wrong.

teachingSections.heading: Bones by region
teachingSections.body:
Head and trunk: the skull encloses the brain, and the part of the skull around the brain is called the cranium. The vertebrae stack on top of one another to form the spinal column, which encloses the spinal cord. The ribs join the vertebrae at the back, and most of them connect to the breastbone (sternum) at the front through short strips of cartilage. Together they form the rib cage, which encloses and protects the heart and lungs.

Upper limb (shoulder to fingers): the clavicle is the collarbone, which runs from the breastbone to the shoulder. The humerus is the upper arm bone. The carpals are the small bones of the wrist, and the phalanges are the bones of the fingers.

Lower limb (thigh to toes): the femur, the thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in the body. The tibia is the shinbone. The tarsals are the bones of the ankle, and the toe bones are also called phalanges.

A memory aid: tarsals and toes both start with t, so the tarsals are the ones at the foot end of the body, in the ankle. The carpals are in the wrist.

teachingSections.heading: Muscles and what joins them
teachingSections.body:
Tendons join muscles to bones. Ligaments join bones to other bones at a joint. Cartilage is a firm, smooth, flexible tissue that covers the ends of bones in many joints.

By mass, the largest muscle in the body is the gluteus maximus, in the buttock. The longest muscle is a different one: the sartorius, a long, narrow muscle that runs across the front of the thigh. The biceps brachii is on the front of the upper arm. The diaphragm, from the heart and lungs lesson, is a muscle too.

teachingSections.heading: The nervous system and the brain
teachingSections.body:
The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and the spinal cord. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) is all the nerves outside them, which reach the rest of the body.

The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain. The cerebellum is a smaller part that lies below and behind the cerebrum. In the words of the body map lesson, the cerebellum is inferior and posterior to the cerebrum. The brainstem connects the rest of the brain to the spinal cord.

teachingSections.heading: Skin: the largest organ
teachingSections.body:
The skin is an organ, and it is the largest organ of the body. With the hair and nails, it makes up the integumentary system.

The outer layer of the skin is the epidermis, and the layer beneath it is the dermis. An organ is a body part made of two or more kinds of tissue working together. The skin’s layers are made of different tissues, which is why it counts as an organ. The word parts from earlier lessons explain the names: epi- means upon, and derm means skin.

Do not confuse the largest organ of all with the largest organ inside the body, which is the liver.

additionalExamples.setup: Where is the cerebellum?
additionalExamples.strong: Below and behind the cerebrum. In anatomy terms, it is inferior and posterior to the cerebrum.
additionalExamples.explanation: Two direction words give two facts. Check each one against its pair: inferior is toward the feet, and posterior is toward the back.

additionalExamples.setup: The longest bone in the body.
additionalExamples.weak: The humerus, because the arm is long.
additionalExamples.strong: The femur, the thigh bone. It is the longest and strongest bone in the body.
additionalExamples.explanation: The humerus is the upper arm bone. The thigh bone is longer, so the femur is the answer.

misconception.wrongModel: The biggest thing inside the body must be the largest organ.
misconception.whyItFails: The skin is an organ too, and it is the largest organ of all. The liver is only the largest organ inside the body.
misconception.betterModel: Read the question closely: “the largest organ” means the skin, and “the largest internal organ” means the liver.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping tendons and ligaments.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Both are tough bands of tissue near joints, so position does not tell them apart. Only what they join does.
commonMistakes.fix: Tendons join muscle to bone. Ligaments join bone to bone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping the carpals and the tarsals.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: They are matching groups of small bones, one in the wrist and one in the ankle, and their names look and sound almost the same.
commonMistakes.fix: Learn them as a pair, and use the letter t: tarsals and toes both start with it, so the tarsals are in the ankle and the carpals are in the wrist.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting the spinal cord as part of the peripheral nervous system.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The spinal cord runs down the back, away from the head, so it can seem to belong with the nerves. It is part of the central nervous system.
commonMistakes.fix: The central nervous system is the brain plus the spinal cord. Everything else is peripheral.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Follow food through the digestive tract and urine through the urinary tract, naming each structure in order.

lesson.title: Food and Urine: The Digestive and Urinary Tracts
lesson.summary: Follow food from the mouth to the large intestine and urine from the kidneys to the outside, and tell apart the tubes and tiny units that are easy to mix up.

content.objective: Put the organs of the digestive tract and the urinary tract in order, say where along each path a structure sits, and tell apart structures with similar names.
content.explanation:
Follow a bite of apple. You chew and swallow it, and it passes the pharynx (throat) and goes down the esophagus, a muscular tube behind the trachea, to the stomach. From the stomach it moves into the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. What is left moves on into the large intestine, and the waste finally leaves the body through the rectum and anus.

That path is the digestive tract: one long tube from the mouth to the anus. Some digestive organs, such as the liver, the gallbladder and the pancreas, sit beside the tube and connect to it, but food never passes through them.

The urinary tract is a second, separate path. The kidneys make urine, tubes carry it to the bladder, which stores it, and one more tube carries it out of the body. Learning both paths in order is the quickest way to place any organ on them.
content.whyMatters: Many anatomy questions ask what connects to what, or where along a path something sits. If you know each path in order, you can answer by position instead of by memorising each organ on its own, and you can see straight away when an answer puts an organ on the wrong path.
steps: Decide which path the question is about: food through the digestive tract, or urine through the urinary tract.
Say the path in order, from start to finish.
Find the structure in the question on that path, and name what comes just before it and just after it.
If two names look alike, such as ureter and urethra, check each one against its place on the path.

workedExample.prompt: A question asks which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder, and a student answers “the urethra”. Is that right? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Yes. The urethra is the urine tube, so it must carry urine from the kidney.
workedExample.strongAnswer: No. There are two kinds of urine tube. A ureter runs from each kidney down to the bladder, so there are two ureters. The urethra is a single tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside of the body. From kidney to bladder is the ureter.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer mixes up the two names as if they were one tube. The strong answer places each tube on the urinary path, which is a reliable way to tell apart names that differ by only a few letters.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Food has just left the stomach. Where does it go next?
choices: The large intestine
The small intestine
The esophagus
The liver
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The small intestine
guidedQuestion.hint: Say the path in order: esophagus, stomach, then what?
guidedQuestion.explanation: After the stomach comes the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. The large intestine comes after the small intestine, and the esophagus comes before the stomach. Food never passes through the liver, which sits beside the digestive tract.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which of these organs sits beside the digestive tract instead of being part of the tube that food passes through?
choices: The esophagus
The pancreas
The stomach
The large intestine
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The pancreas
practiceQuestions.hint: Food passes through three of these. Which one does it never enter?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The pancreas sits beside the digestive tract and connects to it, but food never passes through it. The esophagus, the stomach and the large intestine are all part of the tube that food moves along.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What is the first part of the large intestine called?
choices: The appendix
The rectum
The cecum
The esophagus
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The cecum
practiceQuestions.hint: The appendix hangs from it.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The cecum is the pouch that forms the first part of the large intestine, and the appendix is attached to it. The appendix is a small pouch, not the start of the large intestine itself. The rectum is at the end of the large intestine, and the esophagus is before the stomach.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why is the small intestine called “small”?
choices: It is shorter than the large intestine
It absorbs fewer nutrients than the large intestine
It comes after the large intestine
It is narrower than the large intestine
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: It is narrower than the large intestine
practiceQuestions.hint: Small does not mean short here.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The small intestine is narrower than the large intestine, and that is what small refers to. It is actually much longer. It is also where most nutrients are absorbed, and it comes before the large intestine, not after it.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Villi are tiny finger-like projections. Where are they found?
choices: Lining the small intestine
Inside the kidney
At the ends of the smallest airways
In the brain and nerves
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Lining the small intestine
practiceQuestions.hint: Each of these four places has its own tiny structure with a look-alike name. Which system were villi listed under?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Villi line the small intestine, covering its inner wall. The tiny filtering units inside the kidney are nephrons, the tiny air sacs at the ends of the smallest airways are alveoli, and the working units of the brain and nerves are nerve cells, called neurons.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How many ureters does a typical person have, and where do they run?
choices: Two, one from each kidney to the bladder
One, from the bladder to the outside of the body
Two, one from each kidney to the outside of the body
One, from both kidneys to the bladder
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Two, one from each kidney to the bladder
practiceQuestions.hint: Place the ureter on the urinary path: what comes just before it, and what comes just after it?
practiceQuestions.explanation: There are two ureters, one from each kidney down to the bladder. The single tube from the bladder to the outside is the urethra, not a ureter. Urine always reaches the bladder before it leaves the body.

masteryCheck.prompt: Put the urinary tract in order, from where urine is made to where it leaves the body.
choices: Kidney, urethra, bladder, ureter
Bladder, kidney, ureter, urethra
Kidney, bladder, ureter, urethra
Kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra
masteryCheck.hint: The bladder sits between two different kinds of tube: one brings urine in, and the other carries it out of the body.
masteryCheck.explanation: Urine is made in the kidney, runs down a ureter to the bladder, is stored in the bladder, and leaves the body through the urethra. The other orders put the bladder before the kidney, the bladder before the ureter, or the urethra before the bladder.

teachingSections.heading: The digestive tract, in order
teachingSections.body:
Mouth, then pharynx (throat), then esophagus: the muscular tube that carries food down to the stomach. It lies behind the trachea.

Stomach, then small intestine. The small intestine is a long, narrow, coiled tube where most nutrients are absorbed. Its lining is covered in tiny finger-like projections called villi.

Large intestine: wider and shorter than the small intestine, and most of it is the colon. Its first part is a pouch called the cecum, and the appendix, a small narrow pouch, is attached to the cecum. The large intestine ends at the rectum and anus.

Beside the tract, not part of it: the liver, the gallbladder and the pancreas. They connect to the tract, but food does not pass through them.

teachingSections.heading: The urinary tract, in order
teachingSections.body:
Kidneys: two organs toward the back (posterior) of the abdomen, one on each side of the spine. Each kidney contains a very large number of tiny filtering units called nephrons, which make urine.

Ureters: two tubes, one from each kidney down to the bladder.

Urinary bladder: the organ in the pelvic cavity that stores urine.

Urethra: a single tube that carries urine from the bladder out of the body.

teachingSections.heading: Four tiny units, four systems
teachingSections.body:
Several organs contain huge numbers of one tiny working unit, and the units’ names are easy to mix up.

Alveolus (plural alveoli): a tiny air sac in the lungs.

Villus (plural villi): a tiny finger-like projection lining the small intestine.

Nephron: a tiny filtering unit in the kidney.

Neuron: a nerve cell, the working unit of the nervous system.

When a question names one of these, check which system it belongs to before you answer.

additionalExamples.setup: The appendix is attached to which part of the digestive tract?
additionalExamples.weak: The small intestine, because the appendix is small too.
additionalExamples.strong: The large intestine. The appendix hangs from the cecum, which is the first part of the large intestine.
additionalExamples.explanation: Place the appendix on the path: it is at the start of the large intestine, just after the small intestine ends.

additionalExamples.setup: Where are most nutrients absorbed?
additionalExamples.strong: In the small intestine, whose lining is covered in villi.
additionalExamples.explanation: The large intestine is wider, but most absorption of nutrients happens earlier on the path, in the small intestine.

misconception.wrongModel: The large intestine is longer than the small intestine, so it must be where most nutrients are absorbed.
misconception.whyItFails: “Large” and “small” describe width, not length. The small intestine is the narrower tube, but it is much longer, and it is where most nutrients are absorbed.
misconception.betterModel: Read small and large as narrow and wide. Then place each part on the path: stomach, small intestine, large intestine.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping the ureter and the urethra.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The names differ by a few letters, but the tubes are in different places. Two ureters carry urine into the bladder, and one urethra carries it out.
commonMistakes.fix: Say the urinary path in order: kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra.

commonMistakes.mistake: Putting the liver on the path that food travels.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The liver is a digestive organ, but it sits beside the tract. Food goes from the stomach straight into the small intestine.
commonMistakes.fix: Keep two lists: the tube food passes through, and the organs beside it.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Name the heart’s chambers, tell the kinds of blood vessels apart, and follow the airway from the nose to the alveoli.

lesson.title: Heart and Lungs: Where Blood and Air Go
lesson.summary: Name the four chambers of the heart, tell arteries, veins and capillaries apart, and follow air from the nose to the alveoli.

content.objective: Name the heart’s four chambers and the wall between its two sides, tell arteries, veins and capillaries apart, and follow air from the nose to the alveoli.
content.explanation:
Put your hand flat on the middle of your chest. Behind your breastbone, between your two lungs, is your heart. In the body map lesson’s words, the heart is posterior to the breastbone and medial to the lungs. It is a muscular pump with four hollow chambers. The two upper chambers are the atria (one is called an atrium), and they receive blood coming back to the heart. The two lower chambers are the ventricles, and they pump blood out. Blood passes from each atrium down into the ventricle below it, on the same side. A muscular wall called the septum runs down the middle and separates the right side of the heart from the left side.

Each ventricle sends blood to a different place. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. The left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta, the largest artery in the body, and from there out to the rest of the body. Right and left mean the person’s own right and left, just as in the body map lesson.

The lungs sit on either side of the heart, inside the thoracic cavity. Air reaches them through a branching set of tubes that ends in tiny air sacs, and the diaphragm below them is the main muscle of breathing.
content.whyMatters: Questions on the heart and lungs often turn on one word: atrium or ventricle, artery or vein, trachea or esophagus. Knowing where each structure sits on the path of blood or air lets you tell them apart instead of guessing.
steps: Decide which path the question is about: blood through the heart and vessels, or air through the airway.
Place the structure on that path: what comes before it and what comes after it?
For a heart chamber, say whether it is an atrium (upper) or a ventricle (lower), and which side it is on.
For a blood vessel, ask whether it carries blood away from the heart or back to it.

workedExample.prompt: A student labels a heart diagram that shows the heart as if the person is facing you. They write “left ventricle” on the lower chamber on the left side of the page. Is the label right? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Yes. It is the lower chamber and it is on the left, so it is the left ventricle.
workedExample.strongAnswer: No. When the person faces you, their left side is on your right. The lower chamber on the left of the page is on the person’s right side, so it is the right ventricle. The left ventricle is the lower chamber on the right of the page.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer reads left and right from the page. The strong answer uses the person’s own left and right, which is how every heart chamber is named.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Where does the right ventricle pump its blood next?
choices: The rest of the body
The aorta
The lungs
The left atrium
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The lungs
guidedQuestion.hint: Each ventricle sends blood to a different place. Which one goes to the body?
guidedQuestion.explanation: The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs. It is the left ventricle that pumps blood into the aorta and out to the rest of the body. Blood reaches the left atrium only after it has been through the lungs, so the left atrium is not the next stop.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What are the two lower chambers of the heart called?
choices: The atria
The ventricles
The alveoli
The capillaries
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The ventricles
practiceQuestions.hint: The upper chambers receive blood. The lower ones pump it out.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The two lower chambers are the ventricles, which pump blood out of the heart. The atria are the two upper chambers. Alveoli are air sacs in the lungs, and capillaries are the smallest blood vessels, so neither is a heart chamber.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A blood vessel carries blood back toward the heart. What kind of vessel is it?
choices: An artery
An arteriole
The aorta
A vein
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A vein
practiceQuestions.hint: Arteries and veins are named by direction.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Veins carry blood back toward the heart, so this vessel is a vein. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, arterioles are the smallest arteries, and the aorta is the largest artery, so all three carry blood away.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Put the airway in order, going in from the throat.
choices: Pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, alveoli
Larynx, pharynx, bronchi, trachea, alveoli
Pharynx, trachea, larynx, alveoli, bronchi
Trachea, pharynx, larynx, bronchi, alveoli
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, alveoli
practiceQuestions.hint: The voice box sits at the top of the windpipe.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Air passes the pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi and alveoli in that order. The pharynx is the throat, the larynx (voice box) sits at the top of the trachea (windpipe), the trachea splits into the two bronchi, and the bronchi branch into smaller and smaller tubes that end at the alveoli. The other orders put the larynx before the pharynx, the trachea before the larynx, or the alveoli before the bronchi.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Tiny air sacs sit at the very ends of the smallest airways, each one wrapped in capillaries. What are they called?
choices: Bronchi
Pleura
Alveoli
Atria
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Alveoli
practiceQuestions.hint: They are where oxygen and carbon dioxide pass between the air and the blood.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The alveoli are the tiny air sacs at the ends of the airways. Oxygen and carbon dioxide pass between the air inside them and the blood in the capillaries around them. The bronchi are the larger airways that lead toward them. The pleura is the thin membrane that covers each lung, not an air sac, and the atria are heart chambers.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which structure lies just below the lungs and is the main muscle of breathing?
choices: The pleura
The septum
The trachea
The diaphragm
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The diaphragm
practiceQuestions.hint: It is also the boundary between two body cavities.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The diaphragm is the dome-shaped muscle below the lungs, and it is the main muscle of breathing. It also separates the thoracic cavity from the abdominal cavity. The pleura is the thin membrane around each lung, the septum is the wall inside the heart, and the trachea is the windpipe.

masteryCheck.prompt: Which statement about the aorta is correct?
choices: It is the largest vein, and it returns blood to the heart
It carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs
It is the largest artery, and it leaves the left ventricle
It is a capillary that joins an artery to a vein
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: It is the largest artery, and it leaves the left ventricle
masteryCheck.hint: Which ventricle pumps blood out to the body?
masteryCheck.explanation: The aorta is the largest artery in the body, and it leaves the left ventricle, carrying blood out to the body. It is not a vein, because it carries blood away from the heart. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs, not into the aorta, and capillaries are the smallest vessels, not the largest.

teachingSections.heading: The four chambers and the septum
teachingSections.body:
Right atrium and left atrium: the two upper chambers. They receive blood coming back to the heart, and each passes it down to the ventricle below it, on the same side.

Right ventricle and left ventricle: the two lower chambers. They pump blood out. The right ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, and the left ventricle pumps oxygen-rich blood into the aorta and out to the body.

Septum: the muscular wall that separates the right side of the heart from the left side.

Pericardium: the sac that surrounds the heart. You met it in the prefixes lesson: peri- means around.

teachingSections.heading: Arteries, veins and capillaries
teachingSections.body:
Arteries carry blood away from the heart. The aorta, which leaves the left ventricle, is the largest artery in the body. The smallest arteries are called arterioles.

Veins carry blood back toward the heart. The smallest veins are called venules.

Capillaries are the smallest blood vessels of all, and they connect the arterioles to the venules, forming the bridge between arteries and veins.

teachingSections.heading: The airway, from throat to air sacs
teachingSections.body:
Air comes in through the nose or mouth and passes the pharynx, the throat. Next is the larynx, the voice box. Below it is the trachea, the windpipe, which carries air down into the chest.

The trachea splits into two bronchi, one for each lung. The bronchi branch into smaller and smaller tubes, and at their ends are the alveoli, tiny air sacs wrapped in capillaries. The alveoli are where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged with the blood.

Each lung is covered by a thin membrane called the pleura. Below the lungs is the diaphragm, the dome-shaped muscle that is the main muscle of breathing.

additionalExamples.setup: The trachea and the esophagus both run down the neck. Which is which?
additionalExamples.strong: The trachea is the windpipe, and it carries air to the lungs. The esophagus is the food tube, and it lies behind the trachea and carries food to the stomach.
additionalExamples.explanation: Both are tubes in the neck, so place each on its path: air goes to the lungs, food goes to the stomach.

additionalExamples.setup: The smallest blood vessels in the body.
additionalExamples.weak: Arterioles, because they are the smallest arteries.
additionalExamples.strong: Capillaries. Arterioles and venules are small, but the capillaries between them are smaller still.
additionalExamples.explanation: Arterioles are the smallest arteries and venules the smallest veins. Capillaries connect the two, and they are the smallest vessels of all.

misconception.wrongModel: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood and veins carry oxygen-poor blood, so that is how you tell them apart.
misconception.whyItFails: Arteries and veins are named by direction, not by oxygen. The vessels that carry blood from the right ventricle to the lungs are arteries, yet the blood in them is oxygen-poor.
misconception.betterModel: Ask which way the blood is going. Away from the heart means an artery; back toward the heart means a vein.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping the atria and the ventricles.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: They are different chambers with different jobs. The atria are the upper chambers that receive blood, and the ventricles are the lower chambers that pump it out.
commonMistakes.fix: Link the ventricles with pumping out: both the aorta and the vessels to the lungs leave from a ventricle.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling the trachea the voice box.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The voice box is the larynx, which sits at the top of the trachea. The trachea is the windpipe below it.
commonMistakes.fix: Follow the airway in order: pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, alveoli.

name: Healthcare Ethics
description: Make responsible choices using safety, privacy, and respect.

lesson.title: Reason through healthcare ethics
lesson.summary: Use privacy, consent, safety, and fairness to evaluate scenarios.

content.objective: Use ethical principles to choose a safe and respectful response.
content.explanation: Healthcare ethics often involves balancing values like privacy, patient choice, safety, and professional responsibility.
content.whyMatters: HOSA scenarios may test what you do when the easy answer is not the most responsible answer.
steps: Identify the people affected.
Name the ethical issue.
Choose the safest professional action.
Explain why it respects the patient.

workedExample.prompt: A friend asks about a patient's condition.
workedExample.weakAnswer: Tell them if they promise not to share.
workedExample.strongAnswer: I cannot share private patient information. I would direct them to the proper contact process and protect confidentiality.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The strong answer protects privacy and gives a professional next step.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which principle is involved when protecting patient information?
choices: Privacy
Marketing
Weighing
Pricing
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: Privacy
guidedQuestion.hint: Think about information access.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Patient information should be protected unless sharing is authorized.

practiceQuestions.prompt: What should you do with private patient information?
choices: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
Tell friends
Post it
Guess publicly
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Share only through appropriate authorized channels
practiceQuestions.hint: Privacy rules matter.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Professional ethics requires protecting patient information.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which is an ethical response?
choices: Respect patient dignity
Ignore consent
Embarrass the patient
Skip safety
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Respect patient dignity
practiceQuestions.hint: Ethics centers people.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Respecting dignity supports professional care.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why explain your ethical choice?
choices: To show reasoning and professionalism
To make it longer only
To avoid action
To confuse the judge
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: To show reasoning and professionalism
practiceQuestions.hint: Judges need to see your decision process.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Explaining the principle makes the answer stronger.

masteryCheck.prompt: A scenario involves risk of harm. What principle becomes urgent?
choices: Safety
Advertising
Speaker rank
Budget
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Safety
masteryCheck.hint: Health scenarios prioritize harm reduction.
masteryCheck.explanation: Safety is central when someone could be harmed.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Read what a prefix adds to a term, and tell apart prefixes that look alike or mean opposite things.

lesson.title: Prefixes: Where, When and How Much
lesson.summary: Read the front of a term for position, time, number, speed and amount, then put all three kinds of part together.

content.objective: Say what a prefix adds to a term’s meaning, tell apart prefixes that look alike or mean opposite things, and decode a term that uses all three kinds of part.
content.explanation:
A prefix sits at the front of a term and changes its meaning without changing what the term is about. Tachycardia is tachy- (fast) + cardi (heart) + -ia (a condition): a fast heart rate. Swap the prefix for brady-, which means slow, and you get bradycardia, a slow heart rate. The heart stays the heart.

Not every term has a prefix, so check before you look for one. When there is one, it usually answers one of a few questions: where, when, how many, how fast or how much.
content.whyMatters: Prefixes often decide between answers that look almost the same. A slow heart rate and a fast one differ only in brady- and tachy-, and intra- (within) and inter- (between) look almost identical on the page.
steps: Check whether the term starts with a prefix. Many do not.
Decide what the prefix adds: where, when, how many, how fast or how much.
If the prefix has an opposite or a look-alike, make sure you have the right one.
Put it together with the root and suffix, starting from the suffix.

workedExample.prompt: Intravenous and intercostal both begin with int-. What does each one mean? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Both mean inside. An intravenous line goes inside a vein, and intercostal muscles are inside the ribs.
workedExample.strongAnswer: They use different prefixes. Intra- means within, so intravenous means within a vein. Inter- means between, so intercostal means between the ribs, which is where those muscles sit.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer stops at the three letters the prefixes share. The strong answer reads the whole prefix and then checks it against the root: a muscle can sit between ribs, but not inside one.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What does the prefix in bradycardia tell you?
choices: The heart is enlarged
The heart rate is slow
The heart is inflamed
The heart rate is fast
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The heart rate is slow
guidedQuestion.hint: Brady- is the opposite of tachy-.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Brady- means slow, so bradycardia is a slow heart rate; tachy- would make it fast. Enlargement and inflammation come from suffixes, -megaly and -itis, not from a prefix.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Where is something that is subcutaneous?
choices: On top of the skin
Between two layers of muscle
Below the skin
Across the skin
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Below the skin
practiceQuestions.hint: Sub- is a position prefix. Think about where it puts something.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Sub- means under or below, and cutane refers to the skin, so subcutaneous means below the skin. Epi- would mean upon, inter- between, and trans- across or through.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which term means “outside the cell”?
choices: Intracellular
Intercellular
Pericellular
Extracellular
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Extracellular
practiceQuestions.hint: Four position prefixes, one root. Which prefix means outside?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Extra- means outside, so extracellular means outside the cell. Intra- means within, inter- between and peri- around.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Polyuria describes urine that is:
choices: Produced in large amounts
Not produced at all
Painful or difficult to pass
Tinged with blood
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Produced in large amounts
practiceQuestions.hint: Poly- is a number prefix.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Poly- means many or much, and -uria is a urine condition, so polyuria is urine produced in large amounts. No urine at all would take an- (anuria), and painful urination would take dys- (dysuria). Hematuria is blood in the urine: hemat/o means blood.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A patient has difficulty swallowing. Which prefix would you expect in the term for this?
choices: a-
hyper-
dys-
brady-
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: dys-
practiceQuestions.hint: Difficulty is not the same as absence.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Dys- means difficult or painful, so difficulty swallowing is dysphagia. A- means without, which would describe being unable to swallow at all. Hyper- means above normal and brady- means slow.

masteryCheck.prompt: Put all three kinds of part together. What does polyneuropathy mean?
choices: Pain in one nerve
Inflammation of the brain
Disease of many nerves
Surgical removal of several nerves
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Disease of many nerves
masteryCheck.hint: Start with the suffix, then read from the front.
masteryCheck.explanation: Start at the end: -pathy is disease. Then read from the front: poly- is many and neur/o is nerve. Disease of many nerves. Pain would be -algia, inflammation -itis, and removal -ectomy.

teachingSections.heading: Where: position
teachingSections.body:
sub- means under or below (subcutaneous, below the skin). epi- means upon or over (epidermis, the outer layer of the skin). intra- means within (intravenous, within a vein). inter- means between (intercostal, between the ribs).

peri- means around (pericardium, the sac around the heart). trans- means across or through (transdermal, through the skin). extra- means outside (extracellular, outside the cell).

teachingSections.heading: When, how many and how fast
teachingSections.body:
pre- means before and post- means after (preoperative, postoperative).

mono- means one, bi- two, tri- three and poly- many (bilateral, affecting both sides; polyuria, producing too much urine). hemi- means half (hemiplegia, paralysis of one side of the body).

brady- means slow and tachy- means fast (bradycardia, tachycardia).

teachingSections.heading: How much, and how well
teachingSections.body:
hyper- means above normal or excessive, and hypo- means below normal or deficient (hypertension, high blood pressure; hypoglycemia, low blood sugar).

a- or an- means without (apnea, a pause in breathing). dys- means difficult or painful (dysphagia, difficulty swallowing). mal- means bad or abnormal (malformation).

teachingSections.heading: Pairs to keep apart
teachingSections.body: Some prefixes look alike: intra- (within) and inter- (between). Others are opposites that are easy to swap: hyper- and hypo-, brady- and tachy-, pre- and post-, and ad- (toward) and ab- (away from). Learn these as pairs, so that knowing one tells you the other.

additionalExamples.setup: Hypertension and hypotension.
additionalExamples.strong: Hyper- means above normal and hypo- means below normal, so hypertension is high blood pressure and hypotension is low blood pressure.
additionalExamples.explanation: They are opposites, and the only difference is the prefix. This pair is worth slowing down for.

additionalExamples.setup: Apnea.
additionalExamples.strong: A- means without, and -pnea means breathing, so apnea is a period without breathing.
additionalExamples.explanation: A one-letter prefix is easy to miss. When a term starts with a or an followed by a part you recognise, test whether it means “without”.

additionalExamples.setup: Preoperative and postoperative instructions.
additionalExamples.strong: Pre- means before and post- means after, so preoperative instructions are for before surgery and postoperative ones are for after it.
additionalExamples.explanation: The root is the same in both. The prefix alone moves the instructions to the other side of the surgery.

misconception.wrongModel: Every medical term starts with a prefix.
misconception.whyItFails: Many terms start with their root: gastritis, cardiology and nephrectomy have no prefix at all. Hunting for one makes you split a root in half.
misconception.betterModel: Check whether the first letters match a prefix you know and whether what is left is a real root. If not, the term starts with its root.

commonMistakes.mistake: Swapping intra- and inter-.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Within and between are different places. An intravenous injection goes into a vein; the intercostal space is between two ribs.
commonMistakes.fix: Say the pair together: intra, within; inter, between.

commonMistakes.mistake: Flipping an opposite pair.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Hyper- and hypo-, and ad- and ab-, differ by a letter or two, and brady- and tachy- are easy to swap under pressure. Each pair means the reverse of the other, so one slip reverses the answer.
commonMistakes.fix: Learn one anchor term for each pair: hypertension is high blood pressure, and bradycardia is a slow heart rate.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Use a term’s ending to tell a condition from a procedure or a field, and give its meaning.

lesson.title: Suffixes: What Is Happening
lesson.summary: Read a term’s ending to tell whether it names a condition, a procedure or test, or a field of study.

content.objective: Use a term’s suffix to say whether it names a condition, a procedure or test, or a field or specialist, and give the suffix’s exact meaning.
content.explanation:
The suffix is the ending of a medical term, and it is the place to start reading. It tells you what kind of word you are looking at before you know anything else about it.

Many suffixes fall into three groups. Some name a condition: -itis is inflammation and -megaly is enlargement. Some name a procedure or a test: -ectomy is surgical removal and -scopy is a visual examination with a scope. And some name a field or the person who works in it: -ology is the study of something, and -logist is the specialist. A fourth, simpler kind only turns the term into a describing word: -al, -ar, -ary, -ic and -ous all mean “pertaining to”, as in intravenous (within a vein) and pulmonary (of the lungs).

So even before you know what gastr/o means, gastrectomy tells you it is an operation that removes something.
content.whyMatters: The suffix can change a term’s meaning completely. Gastritis is an illness and gastrectomy is an operation, and only the ending tells them apart.
steps: Read the whole ending, not just its last few letters.
Decide what kind of word it is: a condition, a procedure or test, a field or specialist, or a describing word.
Give the suffix’s exact meaning.
Attach it to the root: the suffix says what is happening, and the root says where.

workedExample.prompt: A practice question asks how a colectomy differs from a colostomy. (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: They’re the same operation on the colon. Both end in -tomy, so both mean cutting.
workedExample.strongAnswer: They share the root col/o, the colon, so the suffix decides. -ectomy is surgical removal, so a colectomy removes all or part of the colon. -ostomy is the surgical creation of an opening, so a colostomy makes an opening from the colon to the outside of the body.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer reads only the last four letters. The strong answer reads the whole suffix, because -ectomy, -otomy and -ostomy differ by a letter or two and name three different operations.

guidedQuestion.prompt: What kind of word is appendectomy?
choices: A condition
A procedure
A specialist
A field of study
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: A procedure
guidedQuestion.hint: What does the ending -ectomy describe?
guidedQuestion.explanation: -ectomy means surgical removal, so an appendectomy is a procedure: the appendix is removed. A condition would end in something like -itis or -osis, a specialist in -logist, and a field of study in -ology.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which suffix would you expect in the name of an operation that removes an organ?
choices: -ectomy
-otomy
-ostomy
-scopy
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: -ectomy
practiceQuestions.hint: Removal, incision and opening are three different endings.
practiceQuestions.explanation: -ectomy is surgical removal. -otomy cuts into a structure without removing it, -ostomy creates an opening, and -scopy is looking inside with a scope.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which term names the specialist rather than the field?
choices: Dermatology
Neurology
Nephrology
Cardiologist
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Cardiologist
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the endings -ology and -logist.
practiceQuestions.explanation: -logist names the person who specializes in a field, so a cardiologist is a heart specialist. The other three end in -ology, which names the field of study itself.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which term names the image itself, not the process of making it?
choices: Electrocardiography
Angiogram
Radiography
Mammography
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Angiogram
practiceQuestions.hint: Process or result: -graphy or -gram?
practiceQuestions.explanation: -gram is the record or image produced, so an angiogram is the image of the blood vessels. The other three end in -graphy, the process of recording.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Osteomalacia and arteriosclerosis describe opposite changes. Which is which?
choices: Osteomalacia is softening of bone; arteriosclerosis is hardening of the arteries
Osteomalacia is hardening of bone; arteriosclerosis is softening of the arteries
Both describe hardening, in two different tissues
Both describe softening, in two different tissues
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Osteomalacia is softening of bone; arteriosclerosis is hardening of the arteries
practiceQuestions.hint: -malacia and -sclerosis are opposites.
practiceQuestions.explanation: -malacia means softening, so osteomalacia is softening of bone. -sclerosis means hardening, so arteriosclerosis is hardening of the arteries. The roots, oste/o and arteri/o, say where; the suffixes say what.

masteryCheck.prompt: What is a rhinoplasty?
choices: Inflammation inside the nose
Repair or reshaping of the nose
A visual examination of the nose
Surgical removal of part of the nose
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Repair or reshaping of the nose
masteryCheck.hint: Rhin/o is the nose. What does -plasty do to it?
masteryCheck.explanation: A rhinoplasty repairs or reshapes the nose: -plasty means surgical repair or reshaping. Inflammation would be -itis, a visual examination -scopy, and removal -ectomy.

teachingSections.heading: Conditions
teachingSections.body:
-itis means inflammation (arthritis). -osis means an abnormal condition (dermatosis). -pathy means disease (neuropathy). -algia means pain (myalgia, muscle pain).

-megaly means enlargement (cardiomegaly). -emia means a blood condition (anemia). -oma means a tumor or mass (lipoma, a fatty mass). -malacia means softening (osteomalacia). -sclerosis means hardening (arteriosclerosis).

teachingSections.heading: Procedures and tests
teachingSections.body:
-ectomy means surgical removal (appendectomy). -otomy means cutting into, an incision (tracheotomy). -ostomy means surgically creating an opening (colostomy). -plasty means surgical repair or reshaping (rhinoplasty).

-scopy means a visual examination with a scope (gastroscopy). -graphy means the process of recording (radiography), and -gram means the record or image it produces (electrocardiogram).

teachingSections.heading: Fields and people
teachingSections.body: -ology means the study of a subject (cardiology, the study of the heart), and -logist means the specialist in it (cardiologist). You may also see the ending written -logy, with the o counted as a combining vowel. The meaning is the same.

additionalExamples.setup: Cardiology and cardiologist.
additionalExamples.strong: Cardiology is the field: the study of the heart. A cardiologist is the specialist who works in it.
additionalExamples.explanation: -ology names the field and -logist names the person. The root is the same in both.

additionalExamples.setup: Neuralgia and neuropathy both involve the nerves. How do they differ?
additionalExamples.strong: -algia means pain, so neuralgia is nerve pain. -pathy means disease, so neuropathy is disease of the nerves.
additionalExamples.explanation: Same root, different suffix, different meaning.

additionalExamples.setup: Electrocardiography and an electrocardiogram.
additionalExamples.strong: Electrocardiography is the process of recording the heart’s electrical activity. The electrocardiogram is the record that process produces.
additionalExamples.explanation: -graphy is the process and -gram is the result, so a question can ask for either one.

misconception.wrongModel: The root is the important part; the suffix is just the ending.
misconception.whyItFails: Gastritis, gastrectomy and gastroscopy share one root and describe three different things: an illness, an operation and an examination. Only the suffix tells them apart.
misconception.betterModel: Read the suffix first. It tells you what kind of word you have, and the root tells you where it applies.

commonMistakes.mistake: Mixing up -ectomy, -otomy and -ostomy.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: They differ by a letter or two, and they mean removing a part, cutting into it, and creating an opening.
commonMistakes.fix: Anchor each one to its origin: the ec in -ectomy means out, so the part comes out; -ostomy comes from stoma, an opening; and -otomy means an incision, where the part is cut into, not cut out.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating -graphy and -gram as the same.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: One is the process and the other is the record it produces, and a question can ask for either.
commonMistakes.fix: -graphy is making it; -gram is what you get.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling every condition an inflammation.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Only -itis means inflammation. -osis is an abnormal condition, -pathy is disease and -megaly is enlargement.
commonMistakes.fix: Say “inflammation” only when the term ends in -itis.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Split a medical term into its parts and read its meaning from them.

lesson.title: How Medical Words Are Built
lesson.summary: Split an unfamiliar medical term into prefix, root and suffix, and read its meaning from the parts.

content.objective: Split a medical term into its parts, say what each part means, and put the meaning back together in the right order.
content.explanation:
Most medical terms are built from a small set of reusable parts. Learn the parts and how they fit together, and you can read a term you have never seen before.

There are three kinds of part. The word root carries the core meaning and usually names a body part or a substance: cardi means heart, gastr means stomach, arthr means joint. The suffix is the ending, and it usually says what is going on: -itis means inflammation and -ectomy means surgical removal. A prefix, when there is one, sits at the front and adds detail such as where, when, how many or how fast: peri- means around and brady- means slow.

Most terms have at least one root and end in a suffix, and many have no prefix at all. Arthritis is just arthr (joint) plus -itis (inflammation): inflammation of a joint. A few terms are a prefix and a suffix with no separate root, like anemia: an- (without) plus -emia (a blood condition). Read literally that is “without blood”; the real meaning is a shortage of red blood cells or hemoglobin, so the parts are a clue, not the whole definition.
content.whyMatters: Nobody memorises every medical term. People who read terms well know the parts and how they fit, so a new word becomes something to work out rather than a blank. The same skill carries into textbooks, health-care conversations and any terminology question you have not seen before.
steps: Find the suffix at the end of the term and say what it means.
Look at the front for a prefix. Many terms do not have one.
Find the root or roots in between, and set aside any combining vowel.
Build the meaning: start with the suffix, then read the rest from the front.
Check that the meaning makes sense where the term appears.

workedExample.prompt: You meet the term gastroenteritis and have never seen it before. What does it mean? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Something to do with the stomach. I recognise gastr, so it’s probably a stomach illness.
workedExample.strongAnswer: Split it: gastr/o + enter/o + -itis. Start with the suffix: -itis is inflammation. Then read from the front: gastr is the stomach and enter is the small intestine. So gastroenteritis is inflammation of the stomach and small intestine.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer stops at the first part it recognises, so it loses half the meaning, including the suffix, which is the part that says what is happening. The strong answer names every part and starts the meaning from the suffix, which is how the definition reads in English.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Which part of a medical term tells you what is happening, such as inflammation or removal?
choices: The prefix
The word root
The suffix
The combining vowel
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The suffix
guidedQuestion.hint: Compare the endings of arthritis and appendectomy.
guidedQuestion.explanation: The suffix names what is happening: -itis is inflammation and -ectomy is surgical removal. The root says where it is happening, a prefix adds detail such as position or timing, and the combining vowel only joins parts together.

practiceQuestions.prompt: How does cardiomegaly split into its parts?
choices: cardi/o + -megaly
car- + di/o + -megaly
cardiom- + -egaly
cardiomeg- + -aly
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: cardi/o + -megaly
practiceQuestions.hint: The root is the part that means heart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cardi/o is the combining form for heart: the root cardi plus the combining vowel o. -megaly means enlargement, so cardiomegaly is an enlarged heart. The other splits cut through the middle of a part, which leaves pieces that mean nothing.

practiceQuestions.prompt: The root gastr joins the suffix -itis. How is the term spelled, and why?
choices: Gastroitis, because a combining vowel is always kept
Gastritis, because gastr never takes a combining vowel
Gastritis, because the vowel drops before a vowel
Gastroitis, because -itis needs a vowel in front of it
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Gastritis, because the vowel drops before a vowel
practiceQuestions.hint: Look at the first letter of the suffix.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Before a suffix that starts with a vowel, the combining vowel drops: gastr + -itis gives gastritis. Gastr does take a combining vowel elsewhere, as in gastroscopy, where the suffix -scopy starts with a consonant. The reason matters as much as the spelling, because the rule is what you use on the next term.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Why does gastroenteritis keep the o after gastr, even though enter starts with a vowel?
choices: The o is part of the root, which is spelled gastro
A combining vowel stays between two roots
Enter always takes an o in front of it
The o stands for “and”, joining the two organs
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: A combining vowel stays between two roots
practiceQuestions.hint: What comes right after the o: a suffix or another root?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Between two roots the combining vowel stays, whatever letter the next root starts with. It drops only before a suffix that starts with a vowel. The o is not part of the root gastr, and it carries no meaning such as “and”.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Reading the suffix first, what does hepatomegaly mean?
choices: Inflammation of the liver
Removal of part of the liver
Enlargement of the liver
Pain in the liver
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: Enlargement of the liver
practiceQuestions.hint: Hepat/o is the liver. What does -megaly add?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Start with the suffix: -megaly is enlargement. Then the root: hepat is the liver. Enlargement of the liver. Inflammation would be -itis, removal -ectomy, and pain -algia.

masteryCheck.prompt: A student decodes pericarditis as “inflammation around the heart”. What should they do with that meaning?
choices: Stop there, because the parts give the full definition
Use it as a clue and confirm it against the context
Replace it with a guess based on how the word sounds
Drop the prefix, because the root and suffix are enough
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Use it as a clue and confirm it against the context
masteryCheck.hint: Is a literal meaning always the whole definition?
masteryCheck.explanation: Decoding gets you close, and the context confirms the exact meaning: pericarditis is inflammation of the pericardium, the sac around the heart. Stopping at the literal meaning can miss that. Dropping the prefix would lose “around”, which is what points to the sac rather than the heart itself.

teachingSections.heading: The combining vowel
teachingSections.body:
Parts are often joined by a combining vowel, usually o, to make the term easier to say. A root with its combining vowel attached, like cardi/o, is called a combining form. The vowel adds no meaning of its own.

Three rules decide whether it appears. Keep it before a suffix that starts with a consonant: cardi/o + -megaly gives cardiomegaly, an enlarged heart. Drop it before a suffix that starts with a vowel: arthr/o + -itis gives arthritis, not arthroitis. Keep it between two roots, even when the second root starts with a vowel: gastr/o + enter/o + -itis gives gastroenteritis.

teachingSections.heading: Read the suffix first
teachingSections.body:
The English meaning of a term usually starts with its suffix. Read the suffix first, then go back to the start of the word and read the rest from left to right.

Pericarditis: -itis (inflammation), then peri- (around), then cardi (heart). Inflammation around the heart. Gastroscopy: -scopy (visual examination), then gastr (stomach). A visual examination of the stomach.

misconception.wrongModel: If I know every part, I know exactly what the term means.
misconception.whyItFails: Parts give you a literal meaning, and the real definition is often narrower. Pericarditis decodes to inflammation around the heart, but it names one specific structure: the pericardium, the sac around the heart. A few parts also carry two meanings, and only the context can say which one is meant.
misconception.betterModel: Use the parts to get close, then confirm the meaning against the context. Decoding is the strongest clue you have, not the final word.

commonMistakes.mistake: Stopping at the first part you recognise.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Gastroenteritis is not just a stomach problem. The part you skipped, enter/o, is half of what the term says.
commonMistakes.fix: Mark every part before you define any of them.

commonMistakes.mistake: Giving the combining vowel a meaning.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: The o in cardiomegaly only joins cardi to -megaly. Treating it as a part sends you looking for a meaning that is not there.
commonMistakes.fix: Set the combining vowel aside, then define what is left.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Recognise common word roots and the body parts and substances they name.

lesson.title: Word Roots: What the Term Is About
lesson.summary: Learn common roots for body parts and substances, grouped by body system, and tell apart the ones that look alike.

content.objective: Recognise common word roots and combining forms, name the body part or substance each one refers to, and tell apart roots that look alike.
content.explanation:
The word root is the core of a medical term. It tells you what the term is about: which organ, tissue or substance. Most roots come from Greek or Latin, which is why they rarely look like the everyday English word. Nephr means kidney. Hepat means liver.

You will usually see a root written as a combining form, the root plus its combining vowel: nephr/o, hepat/o, oste/o. The slash shows where the root ends and the vowel begins.

Roots are easier to learn in groups than one at a time. Group them by body system, and learn each one with a real word you can picture, such as dermatology for dermat/o, skin.
content.whyMatters: The root tells you which part of the body a term is about. If you get it wrong, every other part of your answer is attached to the wrong organ.
steps: Find where the root ends. A combining vowel or the start of the suffix usually marks it.
Read the whole root, not just its first two or three letters.
Name the body part or substance it refers to.
If it looks like another root, check the spelling letter by letter before you decide.

workedExample.prompt: Two terms appear on the same page: cystitis and cytology. What does each one mean? (Our example, not an official test question.)
workedExample.weakAnswer: Both are about cysts. Cystitis is an inflamed cyst, and cytology is the study of cysts.
workedExample.strongAnswer: They use different roots. Cyst/o means the bladder or a fluid-filled sac, so cystitis is inflammation of the bladder. Cyt/o means cell, so cytology is the study of cells.
workedExample.whyItWorks: The weak answer reads both terms by their first few letters. The strong answer checks the exact spelling of each root before giving it a meaning, which is the only way to tell cyst/o from cyt/o.

guidedQuestion.prompt: Nephrology is the study of which organ?
choices: The liver
The kidneys
The nerves
The lungs
guidedQuestion.correctAnswer: The kidneys
guidedQuestion.hint: Find the root in front of the combining vowel.
guidedQuestion.explanation: Nephr/o means kidney, so nephrology is the study of the kidneys. The liver is hepat/o, a nerve is neur/o, and the lungs are pulmon/o or pneum/o.

practiceQuestions.prompt: A cystoscopy looks inside which structure?
choices: A single cell
The skull
A blood vessel
The bladder
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The bladder
practiceQuestions.hint: Check the spelling of the root: cyst/o or cyt/o?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cyst/o means the bladder or a sac, and -scopy is a visual examination, so a cystoscopy looks inside the bladder. Cyt/o, one letter shorter, means cell. The skull is crani/o and a vessel is angi/o.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Enteritis is inflammation of which part of the digestive tract?
choices: The stomach
The large intestine
The small intestine
The liver
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The small intestine
practiceQuestions.hint: Enter/o names one specific part of the intestine.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Enter/o is the small intestine specifically. The large intestine, or colon, is col/o, the stomach is gastr/o, and the liver is hepat/o.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Which combining form would you expect in a term about the ribs?
choices: cost/o
crani/o
oste/o
cyst/o
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: cost/o
practiceQuestions.hint: The general root for bone is too broad here.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Cost/o means rib, as in intercostal, between the ribs. Crani/o is the skull, oste/o is bone in general, and cyst/o is the bladder or a sac.

practiceQuestions.prompt: Pneumonia and pulmonary both refer to which organ?
choices: The heart
The nose
The lungs
The liver
practiceQuestions.correctAnswer: The lungs
practiceQuestions.hint: An organ can have a Greek root and a Latin one.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Pneum/o and pulmon/o are two roots for the lungs, one Greek and one Latin; pneum/o can also mean air. The heart is cardi/o, the nose is rhin/o, and the liver is hepat/o.

masteryCheck.prompt: What does a lipectomy remove?
choices: Part of the lips
Fatty tissue
A gland
Part of the liver
masteryCheck.correctAnswer: Fatty tissue
masteryCheck.hint: Lip/o does not mean what it looks like.
masteryCheck.explanation: A lipectomy removes fatty tissue: lip/o means fat and -ectomy means surgical removal. The lips have their own root, labi/o. A gland is aden/o and the liver is hepat/o.

teachingSections.heading: Common roots by body system
teachingSections.body:
Heart and blood: cardi/o (heart), angi/o (vessel), phleb/o (vein), hem/o or hemat/o (blood).

Breathing: pulmon/o (lung), pneum/o (lung or air), rhin/o (nose).

Digestion: gastr/o (stomach), enter/o (small intestine), col/o (large intestine, the colon), hepat/o (liver).

Bones, joints and muscles: oste/o (bone), arthr/o (joint), my/o (muscle), cost/o (rib), crani/o (skull).

Nerves and senses: neur/o (nerve), cerebr/o (the cerebrum, the largest part of the brain), myel/o (spinal cord or bone marrow), ophthalm/o (eye), ot/o (ear).

Kidneys and bladder: nephr/o (kidney), cyst/o (bladder or sac).

Tissues and substances: derm/o or dermat/o (skin), hist/o (tissue), cyt/o (cell), aden/o (gland), lip/o (fat), hydr/o (water).

teachingSections.heading: Roots that look alike
teachingSections.body:
Some roots look or sound alike and mean completely different things. Slow down on these.

cyst/o is the bladder or a sac, but cyt/o is a cell. my/o is muscle, but myel/o is the spinal cord or bone marrow. hist/o is tissue, hyster/o is the uterus, and hydr/o is water.

One more trap: lip/o means fat. It has nothing to do with the lips, which have their own root, labi/o.

teachingSections.heading: One organ, two roots
teachingSections.body:
Some organs have two roots, one from Greek and one from Latin, and you will meet both. pulmon/o and pneum/o both refer to the lungs, as in pulmonary and pneumonia, and pneum/o can also mean air.

The reverse happens too. myel/o names two different things, the spinal cord and the bone marrow, and only the rest of the term or its context tells you which.

additionalExamples.setup: Enteritis and colitis both describe inflammation of the intestine. What is the difference?
additionalExamples.strong: Enter/o is the small intestine and col/o is the large intestine, so enteritis is inflammation of the small intestine and colitis is inflammation of the colon.
additionalExamples.explanation: Both end in -itis, so the suffix cannot tell them apart. The root carries the whole difference.

additionalExamples.setup: A term contains myel/o. Is it about muscle?
additionalExamples.weak: Yes. My/o means muscle, and myel/o starts with my.
additionalExamples.strong: No. Myel/o is a separate root meaning the spinal cord or the bone marrow, and the rest of the term decides which.
additionalExamples.explanation: My/o and myel/o share their first two letters and nothing else. Read the whole root before you give it a meaning.

misconception.wrongModel: A root means whatever everyday word it looks like.
misconception.whyItFails: Roots come from Greek and Latin, not everyday English. Lip/o means fat, not lips, and a guess based on resemblance can send you to the wrong meaning.
misconception.betterModel: Treat each root as a new word with its own meaning, and learn it with a real term you can picture: lip/o with liposuction, which removes fat.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deciding on a root from its first few letters.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Cyst/o and cyt/o, my/o and myel/o, and hist/o and hyster/o look or sound alike and mean different things.
commonMistakes.fix: Find where the root ends, at the combining vowel or the suffix, and read all of it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming two roots must mean two different organs.
commonMistakes.whyItFails: Pulmon/o and pneum/o both refer to the lungs. Many organs have a Greek root and a Latin one.
commonMistakes.fix: When two roots seem to name the same organ, learn them as a pair.

name: Medical Terminology
description: Explain ischemia and infarction, hypoxia and anemia, and how plaque, a thrombus or an embolus can narrow or block a blood vessel.

lesson.title: When Blood Flow and Oxygen Fall Short
lesson.summary: Learn what happens when a tissue gets too little blood or too little oxygen: ischemia and infarction, hypoxia and anemia, and how atherosclerosis, a thrombus or an embolus can narrow or block the way.

content.objective: Explain ischemia, infarction, hypoxia and anemia, and describe how atherosclerosis, a thrombus and an embolus reduce or block blood flow.
content.explanation:
The body’s tissues depend on a steady supply of blood. The physiology lessons showed that red blood cells carry oxygen, held by hemoglobin, and that the blood delivers it to the body’s tissues. This lesson asks what happens when that supply falls short, either because too little blood arrives or because the blood carries too little oxygen.

Here is the chain in one example. Normally, an artery delivers blood to a region of heart muscle. If the artery becomes narrowed, less blood arrives, and that reduced flow is ischemia. If the flow stays too low for long enough, the muscle cells in that region die, and that area of tissue death is an infarction.

The lesson follows that chain: first what reduced flow and low oxygen are called, then what can narrow or block a blood vessel.
content.whyMatters: Many problems of the heart, the brain and other organs come back to this chain: a vessel narrows or is blocked, the tissue beyond it gets too little blood, and cells are injured or die. If you can place a term on that chain, you can tell apart words that sound alike. This is knowledge for a test, not a way to judge anyone’s health.
steps: Start from normal: which vessel, or which part of the blood, normally delivers the oxygen?
Say what changed: is too little blood arriving, or is the blood carrying too little oxygen?
Follow the change one step on: reduced flow first, then tissue death if the flow stays too low for too long.
Name each step with its term, and check the word parts: hypo- with ox for low oxygen, an- with -emia for anemia.
